newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Heavy rains continue to water Ivorian cocoa.
newsitem.headline: Heavy rains continue to water Ivorian cocoa.

text.p: Heavy wet season rains continued to drench cocoa areas in June with levels in the first 16 days near to the long-term average for the whole month, industry analysts said on Monday.

"If it carries on like this until the end of the month will be double average," said one analyst who put average rain for the period at 207 mm. "That is unlikely but rains are nevertheless good," he added, putting overall wet season rains from April close to long-term averages, excluding June.

Official national weather data for the first 10 days of June show rains averaging 122.6 mm at 10 monitored stations, against 162.9 mm in the previous 10 days and an overall May average of around 233.8 mm.
"Early May was a bit dry but rains picked up to near average by June," said one weather analyst.
Wet season deluges have brought a usual spate destruction to shanty towns and damage to roads in outlying areas of the capital, Abidjan.
Industry sources using their own data said wet season rains in cocoa areas since April were now close to the long-term averages, not taking into account June rains.
Recent rainfall had been strongest in south coast areas, they said.
Wet season rains from April usually peak in June before tailing off into a small dry season in July and August.
July 1996 rains had been nearly double the long-term level as erratic weather patterns had recently blurred the cross-over between seasons, said one industry weather watcher.
Ivory Coast went on to produce a bumper 200,000 tonnes 1996/97 mid-crop (May-Sept) in its record 1.2 million tonnes harvest year (Oct-Sept).

This year's main crop (Oct-April) was close to one million tonnes when the season closed at the end of last month and Swiss chocolate giant Callebaut-Barry, which owns two cocoa factories in Ivory Coast, has put the 1997/98 crop at 1.1 million tonnes.
